opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, because the move felt much more natural to me than it might look from the outside.

During my PhD I worked on physics-based character animation in computer graphics. The goal was to make virtual characters move realistically: walking, running, swimming, even doing acrobatics. To do that you can't just keyframe the motion. You have to build a physics simulation of the body, with joints, muscles or actuators, contacts, and friction, and then design a controller that figures out which forces or torques to apply so the character achieves the motion you want. Once I was deep into that work, I realized it was basically robotics. The only difference was that the robot lived inside a computer.

So the core problems were the same. In graphics I was solving locomotion control, balance, and contact-rich motion. Roboticists were solving those same problems on real hardware. We used similar tools: optimal control, trajectory optimization, and more and more, reinforcement learning. The two communities read each other's papers less than they should have, but the math was very close.

What pushed me to actually make the switch was a growing sense of the limits of graphics. In animation, the result only has to look right. If the simulation is a bit off, or the character gets a little help from an invisible force, nobody notices, and the movie or game is still fine. That freedom is wonderful for creativity, but at some point I wanted my work to face the real physical world, where you can't cheat. If a robot falls, it falls. That honesty was very attractive to me.

I also thought my background could be an advantage rather than a gap. People from graphics are very good at simulation: building fast, stable physics engines and generating huge amounts of motion data. At that time, learning-based methods in robotics were limited because collecting data on real robots is slow, expensive, and the hardware breaks. Simulation offered a way around that. You could train a controller in simulation with millions of trials, then transfer it to a real robot. The big open question was the sim-to-real gap: the simulator is never perfectly accurate, so a policy that works beautifully in simulation often fails on hardware. I felt that someone who deeply understands simulators, including where they're wrong, could help close that gap.

So in a way I didn't leave graphics behind. I took its most powerful tool, simulation, and pointed it at a harder and, to me, more meaningful target: getting real machines to move and act in the real world. Looking back, I think a lot of progress in robot learning came from this kind of crossover, and I feel lucky to have been in the middle of it.

r001.rationale: The response says graphics characters were simulated virtual bodies and that the same locomotion and control problems apply to robots on real hardware—the robot is essentially the real-world counterpart.

r002.rationale: Tan says he wanted his work to face the physical world, where robots cannot be helped by simulation tricks, and describes getting real machines to act in the world as a more meaningful target.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I was doing my PhD, I was working on physics-based character animation in computer graphics. The core problem there is: you have a simulated humanoid or a simulated animal, and you want it to move in a way that looks natural and physically plausible. To do that, you have to solve essentially a control problem. You're not drawing frames by hand; you're designing controllers that take in the state of the body and output torques or forces so the character walks, swims, rides a bicycle, whatever it is.

At some point it struck me that this is almost exactly what roboticists are doing, except their character lives in the real world instead of inside a renderer. The equations of motion are the same. The optimization and learning tools are largely the same. The difference is the output. In graphics, the result is a video that someone watches. In robotics, the result is a physical machine actually doing something.

That realization was both exciting and a little uncomfortable. Exciting because I felt the techniques I'd spent years developing had a much bigger impact potential if they could move from the screen into the physical world. Uncomfortable because graphics is forgiving in a way robotics is not. In animation, if the simulation is slightly wrong, nobody cares as long as it looks right. In robotics, if your model is slightly wrong, the robot falls over. So I knew there would be a sim-to-real gap, and that gap is really where a lot of my later work ended up focusing.

I also saw a kind of complementary strength. The graphics community was ahead in building fast, flexible simulators and in thinking about motion at the level of style and naturalness. The robotics community was far ahead in dealing with real sensors, real actuators, and uncertainty. I thought someone who understood both sides could bridge them, especially as deep reinforcement learning started to make large-scale simulation-based training practical.

So the decision wasn't really a break from graphics. It felt more like a natural continuation. I'd been training virtual legged creatures to move; now I wanted to train real ones. And frankly, the moment you see a physical quadruped get up and walk using a policy you trained in simulation, it's hard to go back to only making videos.

r001.rationale: The candidate says roboticists do essentially the same work as graphics researchers, except the character acts in the real world rather than inside a renderer.

r002.rationale: He says moving his techniques from the screen into the physical world offered much greater impact potential, motivating the transition.

astra-6.text:
I came to see computer graphics and robotics as closely connected, especially when you think about physically simulated motion. In graphics, you might ask how to make a character move naturally in a virtual world. In robotics, you’re asking how to make a physical machine move effectively in the real world. Both involve understanding dynamics and control, but robotics adds the challenge of making those ideas work with imperfect models and real hardware.

That connection made robotics feel like a natural extension of my interests. Simulation could be more than a way to produce an animation; it could be a place to develop and test behaviors that a robot could eventually use. The possibility of taking something from a virtual environment into the physical world was what drew me toward robotics.

r001.rationale: It contrasts motion in a virtual world in graphics with effective movement by a physical machine in the real world, and links simulation to robotics.

r002.rationale: It says the prospect of transferring behaviors from virtual environments to the physical world drew him to robotics, but does not clearly attribute the switch to a desire for tangible real-world impact.

sol-6.1.text:
I came to robotics from computer graphics, where I was working on physically based simulation and character animation. In graphics, you might ask how to make a character move naturally in a simulated world. In robotics, you ask a very similar question, but now that character is a physical machine, and its actions have consequences in the real world.

What attracted me was that connection. Simulation gives you a place to develop and test how a robot moves, but the real world forces you to confront things your simulation may have missed. I saw robotics as a way to build on my background while taking on that additional challenge: moving from generating motion on a screen to creating motion in the physical world.

r001.rationale: It presents robotics as asking a similar motion question to graphics, but with a physical machine whose actions occur in the real world.

r002.rationale: It says the real-world connection attracted him and describes moving from motion on a screen to motion in the physical world, where actions have consequences.
